title: Design a Distributed Key-Value Store (DynamoDB / Cassandra)
tagline: The capstone that ties together consistent hashing, replication, quorums, and gossip into one system.
summary: Consistent hashing, replication, quorums, vector clocks, gossip.

paragraphs: This is the system that stitches together half the distributed-systems concepts. We're building a horizontally scalable store with a simple interface: `get(key)` and `put(key, value)`. The art is in the non-functional guarantees.

blocks.title: Functional
items: `put(key, value)` and `get(key)` over a large dataset (won't fit on one machine).
Values are opaque blobs; access is by key only (no joins, no range scans in the basic version).

blocks.title: Non-functional (the real design)
items: Highly available — accept writes even during failures (lean AP, Dynamo-style).
Scalable — add nodes to grow capacity/throughput linearly.
Tunable consistency — let the caller trade consistency for latency.
Decentralized — no single master / SPOF; nodes are peers.

blocks.text: Name the four pillars up front: consistent hashing (where data lives), replication (durability/availability), quorum (tunable consistency), and gossip + failure detection (membership). The rest of the answer is filling these in.

paragraphs: Data is too big for one node, so we partition it. We place nodes on a hash ring and assign each key to the first node clockwise from `hash(key)`. Adding or removing a node only re-maps the keys in one segment, not the whole dataset — unlike `mod N`.

items.detail: Each physical node owns many points on the ring (virtual nodes). This smooths load distribution and lets heterogeneous machines own proportionally more of the ring. It also makes rebalancing on join/leave spread evenly across the cluster.
Adding a node steals a slice of keys from its ring neighbors only; removing a node hands its slice to the next node. No global reshuffle.

blocks.title: Why this matters
blocks.text: Consistent hashing is what makes the store *elastic*: scaling is incremental and cheap. It's the foundation everything else (replication, routing) builds on.

paragraphs: For durability and availability, each key is replicated to N nodes — the node that owns it plus the next N-1 nodes clockwise on the ring (the *preference list*). If one replica is down, the others still serve the data.

items.detail: Typically N=3. The key's coordinator (first node on the ring) forwards writes to the next N-1 nodes.
Place replicas in different failure domains (racks, AZs) so a single failure can't take out all copies of a key.
Dynamo-style stores are leaderless — any replica can take reads/writes. This maximizes availability but means you must reconcile divergent replicas (see quorums + versioning).

paragraphs: With N replicas, we let the caller tune consistency vs latency using two knobs: W (replicas that must ack a write) and R (replicas that must respond to a read).

items.label: Strong-ish consistency
items.detail: Read and write sets overlap → a read always sees the latest acknowledged write.

items.label: Fast writes
items.detail: Ack after one replica; durable replication continues in background. Low latency, weaker guarantee.

items.label: Fast reads
items.detail: Return from the first replica that answers. Lowest read latency.

items.label: Balanced (N=3)
items.detail: W+R=4 > 3 → consistent, and tolerates one node down on each path.

blocks.title: One system, many personalities
blocks.text: The same store can behave CP-ish (W+R>N, tolerate latency for consistency) or AP-ish (W=1/R=1, maximize availability and speed, accept staleness) — chosen per operation. This is the practical face of PACELC: even with no partition, you trade latency vs consistency.

items.detail: Because any replica can accept writes, two replicas can diverge. Vector clocks capture causality so the system can tell whether one version supersedes another or they're a genuine concurrent conflict. Conflicts are resolved at read time (last-writer-wins by timestamp, or returned to the client to merge — e.g., merging two shopping carts).

If a replica is temporarily down during a write, a healthy node accepts the write *on its behalf* with a hint, and forwards it once the down node recovers. This keeps writes available during transient failures.
To repair replicas that drifted apart (e.g., after a long outage), nodes exchange Merkle trees to efficiently find which key ranges differ and sync only those — avoiding a full data comparison.

There's no master tracking membership; nodes gossip cluster state (who's alive, ring ownership) peer-to-peer. A decentralized failure detector (e.g., phi-accrual) marks nodes down. This keeps the cluster decentralized with no SPOF.

blocks.title: Eventual consistency has teeth
blocks.text: Leaderless + W=1 means a read can return stale or even conflicting values. You must design the application to tolerate this (idempotent, mergeable operations) — or raise W/R for the keys that need it. Don't claim 'strong consistency' for a Dynamo-style store without the quorum caveat.

items.title: Route
items.detail: Client (or any node as coordinator) hashes the key to find its position on the ring and the preference list of N replicas.

items.title: Replicate
items.detail: Coordinator writes to N replicas (cross-AZ); waits for W acks before returning success. Down replicas → hinted handoff.

items.title: Version
items.detail: Each write carries a vector clock so divergence is detectable later.

items.title: Gather
items.detail: Coordinator reads from replicas, waits for R responses.

items.title: Reconcile
items.detail: If versions differ, resolve via vector clocks (return latest, or hand conflicts to the client). Trigger read-repair to fix stale replicas.

blocks.text: This design is essentially Amazon Dynamo. Being able to assemble it from first principles — ring, preference list, NWR quorum, vector clocks, hinted handoff, Merkle anti-entropy, gossip — demonstrates senior-level command of distributed systems. Contrast with a leader-based CP store (Bigtable/Spanner) to show you know the alternative.

cheatsheet: Four pillars: consistent hashing (placement), replication (N copies), quorum N/W/R (tunable consistency), gossip (membership).
Consistent hashing + virtual nodes → elastic, incremental scaling; keys map to the preference list of N nodes clockwise.
Leaderless: any replica serves reads/writes → max availability, but replicas can diverge.
W + R > N → read/write sets overlap → strong-ish read; W=1/R=1 → fast but eventually consistent.
Vector clocks detect causal vs concurrent versions; resolve conflicts at read time (LWW or client merge).
Hinted handoff keeps writes available during transient failures; Merkle trees repair drifted replicas (anti-entropy).
Decentralized: gossip propagates membership/ring state, phi-accrual detects failures — no master, no SPOF.

questions.prompt: Explain how W and R let a caller tune consistency, and give a concrete N/W/R setting for (a) a shopping cart and (b) a financial balance.
questions.hint: W + R > N is the overlap rule; pick per use case.
answer: With N replicas per key, W is how many must acknowledge a write before it's 'successful' and R is how many must respond to a read. When W + R > N, the write set and read set are guaranteed to overlap by at least one replica, so any read sees the most recent acknowledged write — strong-ish consistency. When W + R ≤ N (e.g., W=1, R=1), there's no overlap guarantee, so reads can be stale, but both reads and writes are fast and stay available even when replicas are down.

(a) **Shopping cart**: availability and low latency matter more than perfect consistency, and conflicts are mergeable (union the items). Use N=3, W=1, R=1 — accept the write on one replica, return instantly; reconcile divergent carts at read time by merging. Losing the cart entirely (rejecting writes) is worse than briefly showing a slightly stale cart.

(b) **Financial balance**: correctness is non-negotiable. Use a quorum with N=3, W=2, R=2 (W+R=4>3) so reads never miss a committed write — or better, route money operations through a leader-based, transactional store rather than a leaderless KV. The point of tunable NWR is exactly this: pick per-workload, even per-key.
keyPoints: W+R>N → read/write overlap → no stale reads
Cart: N=3,W=1,R=1 — favor availability, merge conflicts
Balance: N=3,W=2,R=2 (or a transactional store) — favor correctness
Consistency is tunable per operation, not a global setting
followUps: What happens to availability for writes if you set W=N=3 and one node is down?

questions.prompt: Two replicas accepted concurrent writes to the same key during a network partition. After it heals, how does the system know which value wins?
questions.hint: Causality tracking, not wall-clock time alone.
answer: Each value carries a version — a vector clock that records, per node, how many writes that node has applied. When the partition heals and the two versions meet, the system compares vector clocks: if clock A 'dominates' clock B (every component ≥, at least one >), then A causally happened after B and supersedes it — no conflict, keep A. If neither dominates the other, the writes were genuinely concurrent (a true conflict).

For true conflicts, the system can't decide correctness on its own, so it either applies a deterministic rule (last-writer-wins by timestamp — simple but can drop a write) or returns both versions to the client to merge with application semantics (the canonical example: merge two divergent shopping carts by unioning items). Read-repair propagates the reconciled value back to lagging replicas, and anti-entropy via Merkle trees catches anything reads don't touch. The key insight is that wall-clock timestamps alone are unreliable across machines (clock skew), so causality is tracked explicitly with vector clocks.
keyPoints: Vector clocks track per-node causality, not just wall-clock time
Dominating clock → supersedes (no conflict); incomparable → concurrent conflict
Resolve conflicts via LWW or client-side semantic merge (e.g., cart union)
Read-repair + Merkle-tree anti-entropy converge the replicas
followUps: Why are raw wall-clock timestamps insufficient for ordering writes across nodes?
